question.text: A trader buys a call option with strike Rs. 2,200 at premium Rs. 75 and separately buys a put option with strike Rs. 2,200 at premium Rs. 65. Considering each option leg separately (i.e., the break-even for the long call standing alone, and the break-even for the long put standing alone - not the combined straddle break-evens), what is the long-call break-even price and the long-put break-even price respectively?

answer.text: Call BEP: Rs. 2,275 and Put BEP: Rs. 2,135
Call BEP: Rs. 2,135 and Put BEP: Rs. 2,275
Call BEP: Rs. 2,340 and Put BEP: Rs. 2,060
Call BEP: Rs. 2,200 and Put BEP: Rs. 2,200

explanation.text: The Logic: For each leg considered standing alone, NISM Series VIII (pp.66-71) gives: - Long call BEP = Strike + Call Premium = 2,200 + 75 = Rs. 2,275 - Long put BEP = Strike - Put Premium = 2,200 - 65 = Rs. 2,135 The stem expressly asks for the per-leg BEPs, so the long-straddle formulation (which adds total premium to/subtracts it from strike) does not apply. The Trap: Option B inverts the call and put BEPs. Option C (Rs. 2,340 and Rs. 2,060) is the combined long-straddle BEP using TOTAL premium of Rs. 140 (sourced to NISM Series VIII pp.104-106) - it is the correct answer for a different question (the straddle's two BEPs) and was the alternative reading flagged by the audit. Option D ignores premiums entirely. Note: The original stem could be read either as two separate options or as a combined straddle, which made both Option A (per-leg BEPs) and Option C (straddle BEPs) defensible from the workbook. The stem has been tightened to expressly require per-leg BEPs ("considering each option leg separately ... not the combined straddle break-evens"), making the Rs. 2,275 / Rs. 2,135 pair uniquely correct.
